493: /* Return a pointer to the last element of the listpack, or NULL if the
494:  * listpack has no elements. */
495: unsigned char *lpLast(unsigned char *lp) {
496:     unsigned char *p = lp+lpGetTotalBytes(lp)-1; /* Seek EOF element. */
497:     return lpPrev(lp,p); /* Will return NULL if EOF is the only element. */
498: }
499: 
500: /* Return the number of elements inside the listpack. This function attempts
501:  * to use the cached value when within range, otherwise a full scan is
502:  * needed. As a side effect of calling this function, the listpack header
503:  * could be modified, because if the count is found to be already within
504:  * the 'numele' header field range, the new value is set. */
505: unsigned long lpLength(unsigned char *lp) {
506:     uint32_t numele = lpGetNumElements(lp);
507:     if (numele != LP_HDR_NUMELE_UNKNOWN) return numele;
508: 
509:     /* Too many elements inside the listpack. We need to scan in order
510:      * to get the total number. */
511:     uint32_t count = 0;
512:     unsigned char *p = lpFirst(lp);
513:     while(p) {
514:         count++;
515:         p = lpNext(lp,p);
516:     }
517: 
518:     /* If the count is again within range of the header numele field,
519:      * set it. */
520:     if (count < LP_HDR_NUMELE_UNKNOWN) lpSetNumElements(lp,count);
521:     return count;
522: }
523: 
524: /* Return the listpack element pointed by 'p'.
525:  *
526:  * The function changes behavior depending on the passed 'intbuf' value.
527:  * Specifically, if 'intbuf' is NULL:
528:  *
529:  * If the element is internally encoded as an integer, the function returns
530:  * NULL and populates the integer value by reference in 'count'. Otherwise if
531:  * the element is encoded as a string a pointer to the string (pointing inside
532:  * the listpack itself) is returned, and 'count' is set to the length of the
533:  * string.
534:  *
535:  * If instead 'intbuf' points to a buffer passed by the caller, that must be
536:  * at least LP_INTBUF_SIZE bytes, the function always returns the element as
537:  * it was a string (returning the pointer to the string and setting the
538:  * 'count' argument to the string length by reference). However if the element
539:  * is encoded as an integer, the 'intbuf' buffer is used in order to store
540:  * the string representation.
541:  *
542:  * The user should use one or the other form depending on what the value will
543:  * be used for. If there is immediate usage for an integer value returned
544:  * by the function, than to pass a buffer (and convert it back to a number)
545:  * is of course useless.
546:  *
547:  * If 'entry_size' is not NULL, *entry_size is set to the entry length of the
548:  * listpack element pointed by 'p'. This includes the encoding bytes, length
549:  * bytes, the element data itself, and the backlen bytes.
550:  *
551:  * If the function is called against a badly encoded ziplist, so that there
552:  * is no valid way to parse it, the function returns like if there was an
553:  * integer encoded with value 12345678900000000 + <unrecognized byte>, this may
554:  * be an hint to understand that something is wrong. To crash in this case is
555:  * not sensible because of the different requirements of the application using
556:  * this lib.
557:  *
558:  * Similarly, there is no error returned since the listpack normally can be
559:  * assumed to be valid, so that would be a very high API cost. */
560: static inline unsigned char *lpGetWithSize(unsigned char *p, int64_t *count, unsigned char *intbuf, uint64_t *entry_size) {"}

7:  *
8:  * WHAT IS EBUCKETS?
9:  * -----------------
10:  * ebuckets is being used to store items that are set with expiration-time. It
11:  * supports the basic API of add, remove and active expiration. The implementation
12:  * of it is based on rax-tree, or plain linked-list when small. The expiration time
13:  * of the items are used as the key to traverse rax-tree.
14:  *
15:  * Instead of holding a distinct item in each leaf of the rax-tree we can aggregate
16:  * items into small segments and hold it in each leaf. This way we can  avoid
17:  * frequent modification of the rax-tree, since many of the modifications
18:  * will be done only at the segment level. It will also save memory because
19:  * rax-tree can be costly, around 40 bytes per leaf (with rax-key limited to 6
20:  * bytes). Whereas each additional item in the segment will cost the size of the
21:  * 'next' pointer in a list (8 bytes) and few more bytes for maintenance of the
22:  * segment.
23:  *
24:  * EBUCKETS STRUCTURE
25:  * ------------------
26:  * The ebuckets data structure is organized in a hierarchical manner as follows:
27:  *
28:  * 1. ebuckets: This is the top-level data structure. It can be either a rax tree
29:  *    or a plain linked list. It contains one or more buckets, each representing
30:  *    an interval in time.
31:  *
32:  * 2. bucket: Each bucket represents an interval in time and contains one or more
33:  *    segments. The key in the rax-tree for each bucket represents low
34:  *    bound expiration-time for the items within this bucket. The key of the
35:  *    following bucket represents the upper bound expiration-time.
36:  *
37:  * 3. segment: Each segment within a bucket can hold up to `EB_SEG_MAX_ITEMS`
38:  *    items as a linked list. If there are more, the segment will try to
39:  *    split the bucket. To avoid wasting memory, it is a singly linked list (only
40:  *    next-item pointer). It is a cyclic linked-list to allow efficient removal of
41:  *    items from the middle of the segment without traversing the rax tree.
42:  *
43:  * 4. item: Each item that is stored in ebuckets should embed the ExpireMeta
44:  *    struct and supply getter function (see EbucketsType.getExpireMeta). This
45:  *    struct holds the expire-time of the item and few more fields that are used
46:  *    to maintain the segments data-structure.
47:  *
48:  * SPLITTING BUCKET
49:  * ----------------
50:  * Each segment can hold up-to `EB_SEG_MAX_ITEMS` items. On insertion of new
51:  * item, it will try to split the segment. Here is an example For adding item
52:  * with expiration of 42 to a segment that already reached its maximum capacity
53:  * which will cause to split of the segment and in turn split of the bucket as
54:  * well to a finer grained ranges:
55:  *
56:  *       BUCKETS                             BUCKETS
57:  *      [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0) = 11   ==>  [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0) = 11
58:  *      [ 11-76 ] -> size(Seg1) = 16        [ 11-36 ] -> size(Seg1) = 9
59:  *                                          [ 37-76 ] -> size(Seg2) = 7
60:  *
61:  * EXTENDING BUCKET
62:  * ----------------
63:  * In the example above, the reason it wasn't split evenly is that Seg1 must have
64:  * been holding items with same TTL and they must reside together in the same
65:  * bucket after the split. Which brings us to another important point. If there
66:  * is a segment that reached its maximum capacity and all the items have same
67:  * expiration-time key, then we cannot split the bucket but aggregate all the
68:  * items, with same expiration time key, by allocating an extended-segment and
69:  * chain it to the first segment in visited bucket. In that sense, extended
70:  * segments will only hold items with same expiration-time key.
71:  *
72:  *       BUCKETS                            BUCKETS
73:  *      [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0)=11   ==>   [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0)=11
74:  *      [ 11-12 ] -> size(Seg1)=16         [ 11-12 ] -> size(Seg1)=1 -> size(Seg2)=16
75:  *
76:  * LIMITING RAX TREE DEPTH
77:  * -----------------------
78:  * The rax tree is basically a B-tree and its depth is bounded by the sizeof of
79:  * the key. Holding 6 bytes for expiration-time key is more than enough to represent
80:  * unix-time in msec, and in turn the depth of the tree is limited to 6 levels.
81:  * At a first glance it might look sufficient but we need take into consideration
82:  * the heavyweight maintenance and traversal of each node in the B-tree.
83:  *
84:  * And so, we can further prune the tree such that holding keys with msec precision
85:  * in the tree doesn't bring with it much value. The active-expiration operation can
86:  * live with deletion of expired items, say, older than 1 sec, which means the size
87:  * of time-expiration keys to the rax tree become no more than ~4.5 bytes and we
88:  * also get rid of the "noisy" bits which most probably will cause to yet another
89:  * branching and modification of the rax tree in case of items with time-expiration
90:  * difference of less than 1 second. The lazy expiration will still be precise and
91:  * without compromise on accuracy because the exact expiration-time is kept
92:  * attached as well to each item, in `ExpireMeta`, and each traversal of item with
93:  * expiration will behave as expected down to the msec. Take care to configure
94:  * `EB_BUCKET_KEY_PRECISION` according to your needs.

97:  * -----------
98:  * Taking into account configured value of `EB_BUCKET_KEY_PRECISION`, two items
99:  * with expiration-time t1 and t2 will be considered to have the same key in the
